Chapter 3: The Boston Police Strike—A Test of Principle and Public Order.
Sometimes, all it takes is a single event to show us who someone really is. For Calvin Coolidge, that moment arrived during the Boston Police Strike of 1919.
Picture this: the streets of Boston, usually calm and predictable, suddenly plunged into chaos. The police had walked off the job—fed up, demanding better pay and working conditions. Overnight, the city felt exposed. Fear swept through neighborhoods as people realized just how much they relied on those officers to keep order.
Now, most folks in charge would have been tempted to jump in, act fast, maybe even crack down hard just to get things back to normal. But Coolidge, who was governor at the time, saw something bigger at stake. He understood this wasn’t simply about paychecks or overtime—it was about trust. If public employees could walk away and leave everyone vulnerable, what would that mean for the promise between government and its citizens?
So, what did Coolidge do? He didn’t negotiate with the striking officers. He stood his ground, insisting that public safety wasn’t up for debate. At the same time, he called in the state guard to protect the city and keep order. It wasn’t the easiest path—some people were on the police’s side, and lots of folks wanted the whole thing resolved quickly. Still, Coolidge didn’t budge. For him, sticking to principle was more important than giving in to pressure.
Over the next few days, Boston slowly started to heal. The strike ended, and new officers took the places of those who had walked out. Coolidge’s response got attention far beyond Massachusetts. Some people admired his resolve; others thought he should’ve been more flexible. But if you looked closely, you could see his choices were driven by something deeper—a sense of duty, not just to Boston, but to the idea of government itself.
And here’s something to remember: when things are uncertain and tension’s running high, real leadership stands out. Coolidge’s calm and steady hand made a difference. He reminded people that being a leader isn’t about making everybody happy—it’s about doing what’s right, even when it’s tough.
The Boston Police Strike was more than just a headline. It was a test of character—a moment that proved how much courage it takes to stand firm when everyone’s watching. For Coolidge, it was a lesson he carried all the way to the White House, shaping his belief in order, restraint, and the rule of law.
